'''Paul Joseph Black''' {{postnom|country=GBR|OBE|CPhys|HonFInstP}}<ref name=iop>{{cite web|url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/honorary-fellowship/our-honorary-fellows/professor-paul-black#gref|title=''Honorary Fellows: Professor Paul Black OBE, CPhys, FInstP''|website=Institute of Physics|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> (10 September 1930 – 16 March 2026) was a British educational researcher, physicist and a Professor Emeritus at [[King's College London]]. He was Professor of Science Education and Director of the Centre for Science and Mathematics Education at the [[Chelsea College of Science and Technology]] and Head for Educational Studies at [[King's College London]].<ref name=natacam>{{cite web|url=https://naeducation.org/our-members/paul-black/|title=''Paul Black''|website=National Academy of Education|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> Black was the Chair for the Task Group on Assessment and Testing and Deputy Chair of the National Curriculum Council,<ref name=Bera>{{cite web|url=https://www.bera.ac.uk/person/paul-black|title=''Paul Black, Professor''|website=British Education Research Association|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> and is recognised as an architect of the national curriculum testing regime<ref name=indep/> and the national curriculum for Science.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kbCHAgAAQBAJ&q=%22professor+paul+black%22+association+of+science+educators&pg=PA134|title=''Teaching and Learning in the Primary School''|author=Andrew Pollard, Jill Bourne|date=26 September 2002|publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0415102582|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
Paul Joseph Black was born in [[La Cumbre, Valle del Cauca]], Colombia on 10 September 1930, where his British parents William and Susie were living, before moving to Wales.<ref name="obit">{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=Margaret |title=Paul Black obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/apr/27/paul-black-obituary |access-date=27 April 2026 |work=The Guardian |date=27 April 2026}}</ref><ref name="WWW">{{cite web |title=Black, Prof. Paul Joseph |url=https://www.ukwhoswho.com/display/10.1093/ww/9780199540884.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-7697 |website=WHO WAS WHO 2026 |access-date=27 April 2026}}</ref> He completed his first degree at the [[University of Manchester]],<ref name=kings>{{cite web|url=https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/persons/paul-black(b4bb1fc5-3c3d-4ac5-b37c-dc86419f329c)/biography.html|title=''Professor Paul Black OBE''|website=King's College London|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> going on to complete his PhD in [[Crystallography]] at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1954.<ref name=natacam/> Between 1954 and 1976, Black was a faculty member in the Department of Physics in the [[University of Birmingham]].<ref name=natacam/> During his time at Birmingham, he worked with [[Jon Ogborn]] of [[University of Worcester|Worcester College of Higher Education]], designing the [[Nuffield Foundation]]'s [[A-Level]] Physics Course.<ref name=Bera/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chilton-computing.org.uk/acl/associates/users/black.htm|title=''Paul Black and Jon Ogborn, Nuffield Advanced Physics Project''|website=Chilton Computing|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://web.phys.ksu.edu/icpe/Medals/Citations/ogborn.htm|title=''Citation for the Presentation of the ICPE Medal to Professor Jon Michael Ogborn of the Institute of Education, University of London Tokyo 2006''|website=International Commission on Physics Education|access-date=6 February 2021}}</ref> During the early 1970s, Black again worked with Ogborn who was the Project co-ordinator, for ''The Higher Education Learning Project in Physics'' which was funded by the [[Nuffield Foundation]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03075077712331376453?journalCode=cshe20|title=''P.J. Black & Jon Ogborn (1977) Inter-university collaboration in methods of teaching science, Studies in Higher Education, 2:2, 149-159, DOI:10.1080/03075077712331376453''|issue=2|pages=149–159|journal=Studies in Higher Education|date=January 1977|volume=2|doi=10.1080/03075077712331376453|access-date=8 February 2021|last1=Black|first1=P. J.|last2=Ogborn|first2=Jon|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Educational research==
In 1976, Black left the [[University of Birmingham]] and joined the [[Chelsea College of Science and Technology]] as Professor of Science Education and Director of the Centre for Science and Mathematics Education.<ref name=natacam/> Black became the educational advisor to the [[Nuffield Foundation|Nuffield-Chelsea Curriculum Trust]] at this time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nuffieldfoundation.org/news/a-short-history-of-curriculum-development-at-the-nuffield-foundation|title=''A Short History of Curriculum Development at the Nuffield Foundation''|website=Nuffield Foundation|date=18 November 2017|access-date=8 February 2021}}</ref> Between 1978 and 1988, Black was Director for the UK government's national survey of school science performance, and also served on the Research Grants Board of the [[Economic and Social Research Council]].<ref name=icpe/> In 1985, [[Chelsea College of Science and Technology]] merged with [[King's College London]] and Black continued as Professor of Science Education and became the Head for Educational Studies. He held this position until his retirement in 1995<ref name=comment>{{citation|title=''Comment - The College Newsletter'', Issue 153, May 2004}}</ref> becoming Professor Emeritus. From 1985 to 1991, Black was President of the Groupe Internationale de Recherche sur l’Enseignement de la Physique, and became chair of the International Commission on Physics Education between 1993 and 1999.<ref name=icpe/> Black was also a visiting professor of education at [[Stanford University]], and continued to work with the [[Nuffield Foundation]] developing design & technology and science work at primary, secondary and tertiary levels.<ref name=Bera/> In 1986, Black was the president of [[the Association for Science Education]].

During 1987–88, Black was the chair of the Task Group on Assessment and Testing set up by the [[Government of the United Kingdom|UK government]]. The group reported to the then secretary of state for education, [[Kenneth Baker, Baron Baker of Dorking|Kenneth Baker]]. The report produced by the group promoted diagnostic and formative assessment and teachers' professional development and, at a technical level, the use of criterion referencing as the assessment paradigm,<ref>{{cite journal|url= |title=''General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) and the assessment of science practical work: an historical review of assessment policy'', The Curriculum Journal Volume 31, Issue 3 doi.org/10.1002/curj.20|author=Ann Childs, Jo-Anne Baird|journal=The Curriculum Journal|publisher=British Educational Research Association|date=10 January 2021|volume=31|issue=3|pages=357–378|doi=10.1002/curj.20|pmid=33100601|pmc=7566739}}</ref> and produced the original design for national curriculum testing and assessment.<ref name=indep/> In 1992, Black criticised how they were implemented as the Education Reform Act<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/the-annual-meeting-of-the-british-association-for-the-advancement-of-science-in-southampton-hurried-1542503.html%3f |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220525/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/the-annual-meeting-of-the-british-association-for-the-advancement-of-science-in-southampton-hurried-1542503.html%3f |archive-date=2022-05-25 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=''The annual meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in Southampton:"Hurried changes to curriculum will harm pupils"''|work=The Independent|date=25 August 1992|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> {{blockquote|Hurried and sweeping changes to the national curriculum will cause 'serious harm' to children's education}} Between 1989 and 1991, Black was the deputy chair of the National Curriculum Council.<ref name=Bera/> During 1996, Black wrote a report for the [[OECD|Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development]] in which Black stated<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tes.com/news/science-curriculum-should-be-scrapped%3f|title=''Science curriculum "should be scrapped"''|publisher=TES|date=22 March 1996|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> {{Blockquote|the British science curriculum is unnecessarily dull and should be scrapped}} In 1998, Black co-wrote ''Inside the Black Box: Raising Standards Through Classroom Assessment'' with [[Dylan Wiliam]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2011/jan/18/teaching-methods-government-reforms|title=''Teaching guru is optimistic about education''|work=The Guardian|date=18 January 2011|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> Black, along with Wiliam were educational advisors to [[Tony Blair]], giving evidence to the Select Committee on Education and Employment Fourth Report.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200001/cmselect/cmeduemp/205/20520.htm|title=''Select Committee on Education and Employment Fourth Report''|website=parliament.uk|date=8 February 2001|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> In 2013, Black and Wiliam wrote a report that criticised the current assessment, stating<ref name=indep>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/education/education-news/blair-adviser-condemns-a-levels-131187.html%3f |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220525/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/education/education-news/blair-adviser-condemns-a-levels-131187.html%3f |archive-date=2022-05-25 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=''Blair adviser condemns A-levels''|work=The Independent|date=18 December 2013|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> {{Blockquote|A-level grades are an unreliable guide to a student's ability}}

Black was a member of three committees of the [[United States National Research Council|USA National Research Council]], including the [[National Academy of Sciences]] Committee on the Cognitive Foundations of Assessment, and was later a member of the Technical Advisory Group of [[OFQUAL]].<ref name=Bera/> He was also a member of the [[British Educational Research Association]] and the [[National Academy of Education]].<ref name=Bera/><ref name=natacam/>

==Death==
Black died on 16 March 2026, at the age of 95.<ref name="WWW"/><ref name="obit"/>

==Awards==
Black was jointly awarded the [[Institute of Physics Awards|Lawrence Bragg Medal and Prize]] of the [[Institute of Physics]] in 1973 for his outstanding and sustained contributions to physics education, along with [[Jon Ogborn]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold-medals/lawrence-bragg-medal-and-prize-recipients#gref|title=''Lawrence Bragg Medal and Prize recipients''|website=Institute of Physics|access-date=8 February 2021}}</ref> In 1983, his innovative work was recognised with an [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] for services to education.<ref name=iop/> In 1991, Black was made an Honorary Fellow of the [[University of Surrey]].<ref name="Honorary Graduates">{{cite web|url=https://www.surrey.ac.uk/about/people/honorary-graduates|title=Honorary Graduates|website=University of Surrey|access-date=9 February 2021}}</ref> The International Commission on Physics Education honoured Black with their annual medal award in 2000.<ref name=icpe>{{cite web|url=https://web.phys.ksu.edu/icpe/Medals/Citations/black.htm|title=Citation for the Presentation of the ICPE Medal to Professor Paul BLACK, King's College, London, UK Barcelona – Thursday, August 31, 2000|website=ksu.edu|access-date=6 February 2021}}</ref> In 2005, he received a Lifetime Achievement Award for Outstanding Contribution to Science Education, from [[the Association for Science Education]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tes.com/news/paul-black-honoured%3f|title=''Paul Black honoured''|publisher=TES|date=14 January 2005|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref> and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the US National Association for Research in Science Teaching.<ref name=comment/> In 2009, Black won the [[International Society for Design and Development in Education]] Prize for Design in Education (The Eddie)
Lifetime Achievement Award.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.isdde.org/prize/2009-paul-black/|title=''The 2009 ISDDE Prize for Design in Education (The Eddie) Lifetime Achievement Award: Paul Black''|website=International Society for Design and Development in Education|access-date=5 February 2021}}</ref>

* ''Reflections and new directions'' with Robert McCormick, August 2010, Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 35(5):493-499, {{doi|10.1080/02602938.2010.493696}}

* ''Formative assessment – an optimistic but incomplete vision'', January 2015, Assessment in Education Principles Policy and Practice, 22(1), {{doi|10.1080/0969594X.2014.999643}}
* ''Celebration of the past—challenge for the future'', May 2016, Physics Education, 51(3):030103, {{doi|10.1088/0031-9120/51/3/030103}}
* ''Assessment in Science Education'', January 2017, In book: Science Education (pp.&nbsp;295–309), {{doi|10.1007/978-94-6300-749-8_22}}
* ''Helping students to become capable learners'', March 2018, European Journal of Education, 53(2), {{doi|10.1111/ejed.12273|doi-access=free}}
